--- lecture: "a" metadata-files: - ../../_slide-settings.yml format: revealjs: theme: default --- ::: {.t-title} ::: {.t-eyebrow} {{< meta course >}} ::: # Populations & Samples ::: {.t-rule} ::: ::: {.t-meta} Unit {{< meta unit >}} · Chapter {{< meta chapter >}} · Lecture {{< meta chapter >}}{{< meta lecture >}} ::: ::: {.t-attrib} {{< meta attribution >}} ::: ![]({{< meta unit-art >}}){.t-art} ::: # Research Methods ## The scientific method - Uncertainty can be scary, uncomfortable, and dangerous - We strive to **understand** the world and make **predictions** - We often use our **intuition** and **experiences** to do so + Intuitions and experience are usually better than nothing + However, they can often be *wrong* and *misleading!* - We can do much better using the [scientific method]{.b .blue} ::: {.footer} See [*The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Demon-Haunted_World) by Sagan & Druyan ::: ## What is the scientific method? - Start with a **research question** that is answerable with data - Generate a **hypothesis** (i.e., a testable prediction) + Hypotheses usually derive from scientific *theories* + Hypotheses need to be *operationalized* and *falsifiable* - Conduct a **replicable study** to collect relevant data - Analyze the data to **test the hypothesis**/predictions ::: {.footer} The scientific method classically uses experimental studies, but it can also improve observational studies ::: ## Example - **Question:** Does caffeine make you smarter? - **Hypothesis:** Adult humans given caffeine will navigate a maze faster than adult humans not given caffeine. - **Experiment:** Recruit adult humans and give one group decaffeinated coffee and give another group normal coffee. Measure the time it takes each human to navigate a maze. - **Analysis:** Compare the two groups' maze completion times. ::: {.footer} ::: ## What role do statistics play? - **Descriptive Statistics** summarize and visualize the distributions and associations between variables - **Inferential Statistics** allow us to make inferences about our data and quantify the uncertainty in those inferences - **Probability:** Model $\to$ Data
(e.g., given a fair coin, what is the chance of HHHHH...) - **Statistics:** Data $\to$ Model
(e.g., given HHHHH, what is the chance the coin is fair...) ::: {.footer} ::: # Populations and Parameters ## What is a population? - The **population** is **the set of all possible observations** that we want to draw conclusions and make predictions about - Imagine that we are interested in studying sleeping behavior - Are we interested in understanding the behavior of... + All humans who ever lived and ever will live + All adults (18 years and older) living in the USA + All students enrolled in this course this semester ::: {.footer} Populations aren't always made up of people; you could have populations of groups, objects, events, etc. ::: ## How large is the population? - The number of individuals in a population is denoted $N$ + The number of humans in past and future, $N\rightarrow\infty$ + The number of adults in the USA, $N\approx209$ million + The number of students in this class, $N=24$ - We need to be very careful about **generalizing**/extrapolating + Conclusions may not apply to other populations + Predictions may be less accurate in other populations ::: {.footer} ::: ## What is a parameter? - [Parameters]{.b .blue} are things we want to learn about a population + The *typical* sleep duration for students + The *spread* in sleep duration across students - *And beyond (e.g., other summaries, differences, associations)* ::: {.fragment} - A few years ago, I sent out a survey to every student in class - I was able to gather data for this entire population! ::: ::: {.footer} ::: ## Small population example ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ::: {.cell replace_path='["../../data/",""]'} ```{.r .cell-code} # Read in data from file library(tidyverse) sleep <- read_csv("../../data/sleep.csv") # Calculate total sleep hours sleep$total <- sleep$night + sleep$day sleep$total ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8.0 6.0 7.5 9.0 9.0 8.0 6.0 8.0 7.0 9.0 8.0 9.0 6.0 7.5 7.0 7.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = total, data = sleep, geom = "density") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.footer} ::: ## Small population example ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} #### Population Mean The mean represents the "typical" sleep duration $$\mu=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N x_i$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- sleep$total N <- length(x) mu <- (1 / N) * sum(x) mu ## [1] 7.625 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment} #### Population Std. Deviation The SD represents the "spread" across individuals $$\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i-\mu)^2}$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sqdiff <- (x - mu)^2 sigma <- sqrt((1 / N) * sum(sqdiff)) sigma ## [1] 1.038328 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.footer} We denote parameters using Greek letters $(\mu,\sigma)$ or uppercase English letters $(N)$ ::: # Samples and Statistics ## Sampling - In practice, we are often interested in very large populations + $N$ = 209M adults in USA, $N$ = 35T blood cells in body - It would be infeasible to measure such populations entirely - In these cases, we rely on [sampling]{.b .blue} and statistical [inference]{.b .blue} - A **sample** is a subset drawn from a population + $n$ = 600 adults from USA, $n$ = 5M blood cells from body ::: {.footer} Note we use lowercase $n$ to denote the sample size ::: ## Basics of statistical inference {.fs70} :::{.columns} :::{.column} - **Sampling** is drawing a subset of observations to represent a population - **Inference** is learning about the population by studying a sample drawn from it - We first measure *in the sample* whatever we want to know about the population - We call this measure the sample [statistic]{.b .blue} - We use the sample statistic to **estimate** (i.e., guess) the population parameter ::: ::: {.column} ![](../../img/inference.png) ::: ::: ::: {.footer} ::: ## Sample example {.fs70} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} - Our population is all the students in the class $(N=16)$ and our parameters of interest are the mean and SD of their total sleep time $(\mu=7.63, \sigma=1.04)$ - But imagine it is not feasible or possible to survey the entire population... so we randomly select six students to survey ::: ::: {.column .fragment} The `sample()` function will randomly draw a sample (of given size) from a vector *Note that, because sampling is random, we will each get a slightly different sample.* ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} xs <- sample(sleep$total, size=6) xs ## [1] 6.0 8.0 7.5 9.0 7.0 9.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.footer} In practice, we usually *only* have the sample's data and so using `sample()` isn't usually necessary ::: ## Sample example ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} #### Sample Mean The mean formulas are basically identical for both samples and populations $$\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} xbar <- mean(xs) xbar ## [1] 7.75 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment} #### Sample Std. Deviation But the SD formulas are a bit different (we subtract 1 to correct for bias in small samples) $$s=\sqrt{\frac{1}{\color{red}{n-1}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2}$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} s <- sd(xs) s ## [1] 1.172604 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.footer} We denote sample statistics using lowercase English letters $(n, \bar{x},s)$ or Greek letters with hats $(\hat{\mu},\hat{\sigma})$ ::: # Estimation and Uncertainty ## Sampling error - Uh-oh, our statistics $\neq$ their corresponding parameters! :::{.columns} :::{.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(c(mu, xbar, xbar - mu), 2) ## [1] 7.62 7.75 0.12 ``` ::: ::: :::{.column} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(c(sigma, s, s - sigma), 2) ## [1] 1.04 1.17 0.13 ``` ::: ::: ::: - Such differences are called [sampling errors]{.b .blue} ::: {.fragment} - Sampling errors come from two main sources + **Stochastic Error:** The sample was *too small* to be perfectly representative of the population + **Systematic Error:** The sample was *not random enough* to be perfectly representative of the population ::: ::: {.footer} ::: ## Why does sample size matter? - Imagine we had drawn a sample of 2 instead of 6... - We might only sample part of the distribution + The sample mean *would* depend on who was included + We might end up with only extreme people + Our estimate would thus be *more* influenced by chance - Now imagine we had drawn a sample of 14 instead of 6... + The sample mean *wouldn't* depend on who was included + Our estimate would thus be *less* influenced by chance ::: {.footer} ::: ## The law of large numbers {.fs70} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: - Larger (random) samples will tend to better approximate the population - Statistics from larger (random) samples will tend to better estimate the parameters ::: {.footer} ::: ## Small population simulation {.fs70} Let's take samples of different sizes from our population and calculate the sample mean To show the influence of chance, we can repeat this 50 times for each sample size Let's plot each repetition's sample mean as a point (and the population mean as a line) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.footer} ::: ## Large population simulation {.fs70} Do much larger populations require much larger samples? Let's find out... Here is a simulation of sampling from a population $N=1000000, \mu=100, \sigma=15$ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.footer} ::: ## Insights from the simulations 1. Repetitions of a study (with different samples) will result in different estimates due to sampling error 1. There is thus some **uncertainty** in our estimates/inferences due to sampling error 1. We can *quantify* the amount of sampling error in an estimate 1. Larger samples tend to decrease this uncertainty and "stabilize" our estimates (reducing sampling error) 1. Perhaps surprisingly, this depends on the sample's *size*, not on the *fraction* of the population sampled ::: {.footer} ::: ## Sampling distributions :::{.columns} :::{.column} - The **sampling distribution** contains the statistic values from repeated samples - The wider the sampling distribution, the more uncertainty there is - The SD of the sampling distribution is called the **standard error** ::: :::{.column} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](a_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-2.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.footer} ::: ## Standard errors {.fs70} :::{.columns} :::{.column} We can rarely take many repeated samples, construct the sampling distribution, and calculate the SE directly So, instead, we typically *estimate* the SE from the data (just like a parameter) The estimate for the SE of the mean depends on two main things: 1. How large the sample is $(n)$ 1. How spread out the data is $(s)$ ::: :::{.column} #### Standard Error of the Mean $$s_{\bar{x}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}$$ As $s$ increases, the SE increases As $n$ increases, the SE decreases As $n\to N$, the second part $\to$ zero As $N\to\infty$, the second part $\to$ one ::: ::: ::: {.footer} Because we are often interested in infinite populations, the right side of this equation is often left off entirely. ::: ## Example :::{.columns} :::{.column} #### Smaller Sample (n=3) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 3 xs <- sample(sleep$total, n) N <- length(sleep$total) s <- sd(xs) se_m <- (s / sqrt(n)) * sqrt((N - n)/(N - 1)) se_m ## [1] 0.2687419 ``` ::: ::: :::{.column} #### Larger Sample (n=12) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 12 xs <- sample(sleep$total, n) N <- length(sleep$total) s <- sd(xs) se_m <- (s / sqrt(n)) * sqrt((N - n)/(N - 1)) se_m ## [1] 0.1456438 ``` ::: ::: ::: The larger sample thus has a smaller estimated SE ::: {.footer} :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
